summary: Describes the method for encoding Korean characters in both the headers and bodies of Internet mail messages. The method had been in use since 1991 and had become widely used in Korean IP networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Korean letters need a special code to travel in email. This memo writes down the code that people there already used.

questions: how to send korean text in mail
subtitle: Standard encoding for Korean characters in email and message headers.

tldr.problem: Korean mail systems were using different encoding methods, and there was no agreed standard for sending Korean in email headers and bodies according to MIME.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents ISO-2022-KR, an encoding method already in use since 1991 that uses escape sequences and shift codes to switch between ASCII and KSC 5601 (the Korean character set), plus EUC-KR for headers.
tldr.outcome: Korean networks now had an official standard for representing Hangul and Hanja in MIME messages, with ISO-2022-KR for body text and EUC-KR for message headers.

today: RFC 1557 formalized the ISO-2022-KR standard that was already widely deployed in Korean networks. The standard remains in use for legacy systems and specific applications, though modern Korean email often uses UTF-8 and Unicode for better multilingual support and broader character coverage.

sections.title: Documenting an Existing Standard
sections.content: Korean mail systems had been using a particular encoding method since 1991, and it had become widely adopted across Korean IP networks. However, no official RFC documented the method or aligned it with MIME standards. This document standardizes that de-facto practice, specifying how to represent Korean characters in both the headers and bodies of Internet mail messages. The encoding method assumes messages begin in ASCII and use shift functions to switch to KSC 5601, the Korean character set that includes Hangul (the native alphabet), Hanja (Chinese ideographic characters), and graphics.
sections.plainLanguage: Korea was already using a way to send Korean letters in email, but it was not officially written down. This memo documents that method.

sections.title: The ISO-2022-KR Encoding
sections.content: ISO-2022-KR uses three key control codes to switch between ASCII and Korean text: the escape sequence ESC $ ) C (which appears once at the beginning of a line before any Korean characters), SO (shift out) to begin Korean text, and SI (shift in) to return to ASCII. KSC 5601 characters are two bytes long, allowing representation of Hangul, Hanja, and other symbols. The escape sequence appears once at the start of a line, and then SO-SI pairs mark boundaries between Korean and ASCII throughout the message. The encoding is inherently 7-bit, so no additional Content-Transfer-Encoding is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Special codes say 'Korean text starts here' and 'back to English now.' Each Korean letter takes two bytes.

sections.title: MIME Declarations and Header Encoding
sections.content: For the message body, the Content-Type header specifies charset=iso-2022-kr, and Content-Transfer-Encoding can be omitted since the encoding is 7-bit. For message headers, Korean must be encoded differently using EUC-KR (Extended Unix Code for Korean), which is 8-bit. Header text is then further encoded using the B-encoding (Base64) or Q-encoding (Quoted-Printable) methods defined in RFC 1522. This two-level encoding (EUC-KR inside B/Q encoding) allows mail clients to display Korean names and subjects in message headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The message body uses one type of encoding, and the header (with names and subjects) uses a different type.
